[2022 fall ms math-stat — problem 3]

Two COVID-19 vaccines (A, B) and a control: $n$ observations from group A, $m$ from B, $k$ from control. Overall mean $\mu$, group effects $\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$. (1) Write a regression model for the vaccination effects. (2) Give the corresponding model matrix. (3) Can all of $\mu, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3$ be estimated? If not, why, and give a fix.

response.text:
Let the observations be ordered as

\[
Y=\bigl(Y_{A1},\dots,Y_{An},Y_{B1},\dots,Y_{Bm},Y_{C1},\dots,Y_{Ck}\bigr)^T,
\]

where \(C\) denotes control, and assume \(n,m,k\ge 1\).

## (1) Regression/ANOVA model

A natural one-way ANOVA regression model is

\[
Y_{gi}=\mu+\alpha_g+\varepsilon_{gi}, \qquad g=1,2,3,
\]

where group \(1\) is vaccine A, group \(2\) is vaccine B, and group \(3\) is control. Thus explicitly,

\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{Ai} &= \mu+\alpha_1+\varepsilon_{Ai}, \qquad i=1,\dots,n,\\
Y_{Bj} &= \mu+\alpha_2+\varepsilon_{Bj}, \qquad j=1,\dots,m,\\
Y_{C\ell} &= \mu+\alpha_3+\varepsilon_{C\ell}, \qquad \ell=1,\dots,k.
\end{aligned}
\]

Usually one assumes

\[
\varepsilon_{gi}\stackrel{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,\sigma^2),
\]

or at least mean \(0\), variance \(\sigma^2\), independent errors.

In vector form,

\[
Y=X\theta+\varepsilon,
\qquad 
\theta=(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)^T.
\]

---

## (2) Model matrix

With the ordering above, the model matrix is

\[
X=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 0_n & \mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 1_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 1_k
\end{pmatrix},
\]

where \(\mathbf 1_r\) is an \(r\)-vector of ones and \(\mathbf 0_r\) is an \(r\)-vector of zeros.

Equivalently, the rows are

\[
(1,1,0,0) \quad \text{for vaccine A},
\]

\[
(1,0,1,0) \quad \text{for vaccine B},
\]

\[
(1,0,0,1) \quad \text{for control}.
\]

---

## (3) Can all of \(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3\) be estimated?

No. The parameters are not jointly identifiable.

The reason is that the intercept column is the sum of the three group indicator columns:

\[
\mathbf 1_{n+m+k}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n\\
\mathbf 1_m\\
\mathbf 1_k
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n\\
\mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 0_k
\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m\\
\mathbf 0_k
\end{pmatrix}
+
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 0_m\\
\mathbf 1_k
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Therefore the columns of \(X\) are linearly dependent. In fact,

\[
X(1,-1,-1,-1)^T=0.
\]

So \(X\) has rank \(3\), not \(4\), and \(X^TX\) is singular. Equivalently, for any constant \(c\),

\[
\mu+\alpha_g
=
(\mu+c)+(\alpha_g-c),
\]

so the fitted group means are unchanged by replacing

\[
(\mu,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)
\]

with

\[
(\mu+c,\alpha_1-c,\alpha_2-c,\alpha_3-c).
\]

Thus the decomposition into an overall mean plus three group effects is not unique.

What is estimable are the three group means

\[
\mu+\alpha_1,\qquad \mu+\alpha_2,\qquad \mu+\alpha_3,
\]

and contrasts such as

\[
\alpha_1-\alpha_3, \qquad \alpha_2-\alpha_3, \qquad \alpha_1-\alpha_2.
\]

---

## A standard fix

One fix is to impose an identifiability constraint. For vaccine-control comparisons, the most natural choice is to take the control group as the reference level by setting

\[
\alpha_3=0.
\]

Then the model becomes

\[
\begin{aligned}
Y_{Ai} &= \beta_0+\tau_A+\varepsilon_{Ai},\\
Y_{Bj} &= \beta_0+\tau_B+\varepsilon_{Bj},\\
Y_{C\ell} &= \beta_0+\varepsilon_{C\ell},
\end{aligned}
\]

where

\[
\beta_0=\mu+\alpha_3
\]

is the control mean,

\[
\tau_A=\alpha_1-\alpha_3
\]

is the vaccine A effect relative to control, and

\[
\tau_B=\alpha_2-\alpha_3
\]

is the vaccine B effect relative to control.

The corresponding full-rank model matrix is

\[
X_{\text{ref}}=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 1_n & \mathbf 0_n\\
\mathbf 1_m & \mathbf 0_m & \mathbf 1_m\\
\mathbf 1_k & \mathbf 0_k & \mathbf 0_k
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

This matrix has rank \(3\) provided \(n,m,k\ge 1\). The least squares estimates are then

\[
\widehat{\beta}_0=\bar Y_C,
\]

\[
\widehat{\tau}_A=\bar Y_A-\bar Y_C,
\]

\[
\widehat{\tau}_B=\bar Y_B-\bar Y_C.
\]

Another common fix is to impose a sum-to-zero constraint such as

\[
\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3=0,
\]

or, for an unbalanced design if \(\mu\) is meant to be the sample-size-weighted overall mean,

\[
n\alpha_1+m\alpha_2+k\alpha_3=0.
\]

Any such independent constraint removes the non-identifiability.
